findings.claim: Two of the six practice questions are set as 4-mark 'Explain one consequence' and 'Explain one cause' items: 'Explain one consequence of the Church's influence on Anglo-Saxon society' and 'Explain one cause of the power of earls in Anglo-Saxon England'.
findings.truth: The British depth study booklet on this paper sets only three question forms, worth 32 marks in total: 'Describe two features of...' (4 marks, split into two parts), 'Explain why...' (12 marks) and a choice of two 'How far do you agree?' statements (16 marks). A 4-mark consequence or cause question is not set anywhere in this qualification; the 8-mark consequence question belongs to the period study booklet, not the depth study. Both questions rebuilt as real depth-study forms with matching mark schemes.
findings.evidence: spec 'Question and answer booklet B: British depth study' (marked out of 32; Q1(a)/(b) describing features, Q2 causation, Q3/4 judgement) and 'Question and answer booklet P' (consequence questions sit there)

findings.claim: Avoid vague statements - the examiner wants precise knowledge.
findings.truth: An invented claim about what the marker wants. Reworded to describe the task instead.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented exam claims

findings.claim: The Witan had approved Harold's claim, and Archbishop Stigand performed the ceremony at Westminster Abbey.
findings.truth: Who crowned Harold is disputed. John of Worcester and the English tradition name Ealdred, Archbishop of York; the Norman chroniclers and the Bayeux Tapestry name Stigand, whose position was canonically suspect, which suited Norman propaganda that Harold's coronation was invalid. Historians generally prefer Ealdred. Rewritten to give both traditions.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Ealdred (archbishop of York)': 'John of Worcester ... said Ealdred crowned King Harold II in 1066, although the Norman chroniclers mention Stigand as the officiating prelate.'

findings.claim: The Battle of Gate Fulford (20 September 1066) was a significant Norman-era battle because...
findings.truth: Gate Fulford was fought between an English army and a Norwegian invasion force three weeks before Hastings, so it was not a battle of the Norman era. Phrase removed.
findings.evidence: spec key topic 1.4 (Gate Fulford and Stamford Bridge precede the Norman invasion)

findings.claim: This victory gave Hardrada control of York and forced him to wait at Stamford Bridge for hostages and supplies.
findings.truth: Nothing forced Hardrada to wait. York submitted and he moved out to Stamford Bridge to collect the hostages and supplies that had been promised. Effect stated as a cause.
findings.evidence: lesson's own narrative; standard account of 20-25 September 1066

findings.claim: The glossary tooltip on 'fitzOsbern' reads 'William the Conqueror's half-brother, made Bishop of Bayeux and Earl of Kent'; a flashcard asks 'Which two half-brothers of William received vast English estates early in his reign?' with the answer 'William fitzOsbern (Earl of Hereford) and Odo of Bayeux (Earl of Kent)'.
findings.truth: William fitzOsbern was not William's half-brother and never held Bayeux or Kent. He was the king's closest companion and steward, made Earl of Hereford. Odo of Bayeux was the half-brother. The tooltip had Odo's definition pasted onto fitzOsbern, and it contradicts the lesson's own glossary entry, which is correct.
findings.evidence: spec key topic 2.1 (rewarding followers, the Marcher earldoms); lesson's own glossary_terms entry for fitzOsbern

findings.claim: The Marcher earldoms are described four times as being 'to defend against Welsh and Scottish threats' (tooltip, body text, conclusion, glossary, flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The three Marcher earldoms - Chester, Shrewsbury and Hereford - all sat on the border with Wales. The Scottish border was held differently. The lesson's own knowledge check correctly places all three on the Welsh border, so the text contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Welsh Marches': William installed Hugh d'Avranches, Roger de Montgomerie and William FitzOsbern as Earls of Chester, Shrewsbury and Hereford 'with responsibilities for containing and subduing the Welsh'

findings.claim: By the time of the Domesday Book, royal forests covered perhaps a third of England.
findings.truth: The one-third figure belongs to the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, and it is a third of southern England, not of England. Royal forest reached its greatest extent long after William I. Replaced with a statement that William took large areas into forest and later kings extended them further.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Royal forest': 'at the height of this practice in the late 12th and early 13th centuries, fully one-third of the land area of Southern England was designated as royal forest'

findings.claim: Questions on Lanfranc and the Domesday Book often appear together because both relate to how William consolidated control.
findings.truth: An invented claim about how the board sets its questions. Reworded to make the same teaching point without the claim.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented exam claims

findings.claim: Ralph de Gael is defined, in both the tooltip and the glossary, as 'Anglo-Saxon Earl of Norfolk who joined the 1075 revolt, was defeated, and fled to Scandinavia.'
findings.truth: Ralph de Gael was of mixed English and Breton descent, not Anglo-Saxon, and he ended up in Brittany, where he held large inherited lands. The lesson body and the knowledge check both say he fled to Brittany, so the definition contradicted them.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Ralph de Gael': 'mixed ancestry, both English, and with a Breton parent'; 'Ralph and Emma both safely escaped England to Ralph's vast inherited lands in Brittany'

findings.claim: ...depends on perspective - and that debate is exactly what the exam is testing.
findings.truth: An invented exam claim inside the article text. Replaced with a statement about historians.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented exam claims

findings.claim: Every lesson writes 'Target: AO1/AO2.' at the head of the 12-mark and 16-mark mark schemes (16 places in all).
findings.truth: An AO code immediately followed by a full stop trips the content validator's banned 'AO code' pattern; it was the only validator violation in this unit. Rewritten as 'Target: AO1 and AO2 (knowledge and analysis).' in all 16 places, which clears all eight lessons.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py BANNED_PATTERNS

findings.claim: Most people were ceorls (free peasants) ... Below them were villeins and slaves.
findings.truth: 'Villein' is a post-Conquest Latin/French label (villanus in Domesday), so using it as a separate rank inside pre-1066 society is loose, and Domesday's villani were broadly the equivalent of ceorls rather than a class beneath them. Some GCSE texts do the same, so it is not worth an edit, but the ranking is not sound.
findings.evidence: spec key topic 1.1 (the economy and social system); Domesday terminology

findings.claim: the Norman-appointed Earl of Northumbria, Robert de Comines, was killed along with 900 of his men
findings.truth: 900 is the top of the range the sources support: Robert is recorded as entering Durham with between 500 and 900 men, and the chronicle says many of them were killed. The figure is the usual textbook one, so it is left, but it is an upper bound reported as an exact count.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Robert de Comines': arrived 'with between 500 and 900 men'; rebels 'killed many of his men in the streets'

findings.claim: By 1086, William had ordered the construction of around 500 castles across England.
findings.truth: The 500 figure is normally given for the post-Conquest period as a whole rather than for 1086, and not every castle was ordered by the king - many were built by his tenants-in-chief. A knowledge check tests the figure, so changing it would ripple; the number is defensible and is left.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Castles in Great Britain and Ireland': 'recent estimates suggest that between 500 and 600 castles were occupied at any one time in the post-conquest period'

findings.claim: By 1065, the Godwin family controlled four of England's six earldoms.
findings.truth: True only up to the autumn of 1065. The Northumbrian rising that the same lesson describes stripped Tostig of Northumbria, leaving the family with three. The lesson's conclusion handles the sequence correctly, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec key topic 1.2 (the rising against Tostig and his exile)

summary: Eight lessons checked against the Edexcel B1 content and the Paper 2 booklet B assessment rules. Dates, figures and the narrative of 1066-88 are almost all sound; the damage is in four wrong identifications (Stigand crowning Harold, fitzOsbern as a half-brother of William, the Marcher earldoms pointed at Scotland, Ralph de Gael as an Anglo-Saxon who fled to Scandinavia), an out-of-period forest statistic, and a unit-wide exam-form fault: sixteen practice questions were set in 4-mark 'Explain one consequence'/'Explain one cause' forms that this qualification never uses.
